description: The HOOK BANK: pre-approved, in-voice, claim-safe opening lines and captions, grouped by the PSYCHOLOGICAL MECHANISM they exercise so the loop can A/B mechanisms against each other rather than individual lines. Adapted (never pasted) from an external viral-hook pack; every line here was rewritten into the SFFS voice against brand/brand-voice.md + brand/brand-voice-examples.json. Read by the hook A/B arm (hermes/src/dimensions.ts) and by caption generation (hermes/src/design.ts makeCaption). See ab-testing/README.md for the schema and the claim rules.

purpose.problem: Median skip rate is 77.2% in the first three seconds. The opening line and first plate are the only surfaces that fight it.

surfaces.opening: The spoken opener + the plate it burns in, BEFORE question one. High value: this is what fights the 77.2%.
surfaces.caption: The post caption. Near-zero retention effect, but free to improve and required to be novel (see publishGate NOVELTY_WINDOW).

purpose.why_mechanisms_not_lines: Individual lines are noise at our sample sizes. Grouping by mechanism means an arm can be scored on n>=5 posts (content-defaults.json promotion.min_sample) with the wording varied inside the arm, so a win is attributable to the mechanism and not to one lucky sentence.

claim_rules.the_line: A number attached to HOW HARD THE QUESTION IS is in policy. A number attached to WHAT THE PRODUCT DOES FOR THE VIEWER is not. That is the whole rule, and it is a real distinction rather than a hedge: difficulty framing is genre convention that nobody reads as data, while an efficacy claim about the app is the kind that actually gets challenged.

owner_approval.decision: Unmeasured numeric difficulty claims about the question ('97% get this wrong', 'only 3% spot it', '9 out of 10 pick B') are APPROVED and are a first-class category, not an edge case. They are understood as difficulty framing and are standard for the format.
owner_approval.note: This is a recorded decision, not an oversight. compliance.md section 3 ('nothing misleading about difficulty, odds') reads conservatively on its face; the owner has scoped it to product and outcome claims, where it still binds hard. Anyone tightening this later should change it here rather than quietly re-filtering the bank.

allowed_claim_classes.stated-stat: An unmeasured numeric or quantified claim about how hard THE QUESTION is. The approved pattern. Attaches to the puzzle or to the viewer's odds on the puzzle, never to the product.
allowed_claim_classes.none: Asserts nothing. Imperatives, questions, dares, and rules we ourselves define.
allowed_claim_classes.opinion: A subjective judgement about OUR OWN puzzle ('this one is sneaky'). Brand-native: the host says 'and this one is tricky!' and 'it's sneaky!' verbatim in the corpus. This is the no-number counterpart to stated-stat and the natural A/B partner for it.
allowed_claim_classes.self-verifiable: A fact about THIS video readable straight off the render props (question count, countdown seconds, whether the last answer is withheld). True by construction; `requires` pins the props it depends on.
allowed_claim_classes.measured: A real statistic with a stated population and n. Not required, and nothing here depends on it, but strictly better than an invented number if we ever cheaply have one. See numeric_claims.upgrade_path.

banned_claim_classes.product-efficacy: Any claim about what the app, the brand, or the videos DO for the viewer. '97% of players raise their score', 'users get smarter in a week', 'watch daily and your IQ goes up'. Different category from difficulty framing, genuinely challengeable, and not what was asked for. If a source hook made an outcome claim, the number was moved onto the question's difficulty or the hook was dropped.
banned_claim_classes.authority-result: First-person performance brags ('this method got me a 92% retention rate'). Structurally unavailable to us anyway: we are a game show, not a person with results. 26 of the 69 numeric hooks in the source pack are this shape.
banned_claim_classes.per-item-contradiction: Anything true only for SOME questions when the specific option is not controlled: 'the obvious answer is wrong', 'there is a trap in here'. Excluded for INTERNAL CONSISTENCY, not for legal reasons. The bank attaches to a randomly selected item, so a hook that pre-judges the answer will contradict its own reveal roughly whenever it guesses wrong, which makes us look sloppy on camera. Lines that name a specific option are allowed only with a `fill` block so the selector can pick a letter that is genuinely NOT the answer.

numeric_claims.status: APPROVED for question difficulty. See claim_rules.owner_approval.
numeric_claims.how_numbers_are_chosen: Magnitude is varied on purpose across the stated-difficulty-stat entries (1%, 3%, 8%, 12%, 30%, 70%, 88%, 97%, 9-in-10). Extreme numbers are more dramatic, moderate ones more believable, and which direction wins is a real sub-axis worth reading once the arm has volume. Do not collapse them all to 97%.
evidence: content/master-question-bank.json (1544 entries) has no difficulty field. `tier` is the question TYPE (ODD ONE OUT, NUMBER SERIES, ...), not a difficulty rating.
hermes/src/gates.ts asks the rubric LLM for a difficulty label (easy|medium|hard|off) but it is a model opinion used to reject items, is not persisted per question, and is not a human failure rate.
ab-testing/ab-database.json: 10 comments total across the 15 posts that have metrics. No per-question response data of any kind.
upgrade_path: Nothing here waits on this. But a real number is strictly better than an invented one at the same cost, so if either route below gets executed, swap the figure and set claim_class to `measured` with the population, n, and date in a `claim_evidence` field.

GRADE THE COMMENTS. The cliffhanger default already withholds the last answer and asks for it, and ab-testing/comment-reply-guide.md already grades a commenter against the answer key. Persisting that grade per (post, question) yields a real failure rate. The population is always 'people who commented on this post', never 'people'. Needs roughly n=100 per item, which is far off at current comment volume.

NORM THE ITEM DELIBERATELY. Put the exact item in front of a known sample before it ships (an Instagram Stories poll on our own audience, or a small paid panel). This is the only route that yields a defensible 'X% of N people got this wrong', and it is cheap for the handful of items a difficulty-stat arm actually needs.

conventions.opening.vo: Spoken by the cloned host voice. Write it exactly as it should be SPOKEN: no digits (the intro beat builder must run text through n2w like narration.ts planBeats does, so words avoid surprises), no symbols, one or two short sentences, roughly 1.0 to 2.0 seconds. The synthesizer adds the `[excited]` tag, same as planBeats. This is why every stat is spelled out in `vo` ('Ninety seven percent') and written as a numeral on the plate ('97%'): the plate wants the glance-readable form and the voice wants the speakable one.
conventions.fill: Present only on lines that name a specific answer option. The selector must substitute every placeholder before render, using an option letter that is NOT the answer. A line with an unresolved or wrongly-resolved placeholder must never ship: it would contradict its own reveal on camera.
conventions.opening.plate.title: ALL CAPS, Anton, <= 20 characters. Matches the existing on-screen convention (SMART or FART?, ONLY 1% PASS, ARE YOU SMART OR FART?).
conventions.opening.plate.subtitle: lowercase casual, <= 32 characters.
conventions.opening.emoji: NONE. Plates in this brand carry no emoji.
conventions.caption.body: <= 180 characters before hashtags (the ceiling hermes/src/design.ts makeCaption enforces). Hashtags are appended per-post from the rotating set A/B/C, not stored here.
conventions.caption.emoji: AT MOST ONE Extended_Pictographic codepoint. This is stricter than it reads: brand/brand-voice.md says the combined glyph counts as one emoji, but brand.ts ruleCheckCopy counts codepoints, so the two-codepoint brain+wind glyph fails the gate on its own and fails harder next to a pointing finger. Historical captions in the corpus predate that gate. Every caption here uses exactly one pointing-finger emoji and never the combined glyph.
conventions.caption.nudge: Every caption ends on a follow or come-back nudge. Non-negotiable per brand/brand-voice.md section 3.
conventions.opening.nudge: Openings deliberately carry NO nudge: the nudge belongs at the end of the video, where the existing endcard already delivers it (defaultOutro). Front-loading a follow ask into the first second would spend the three seconds we are trying to win.
conventions.dashes: No em dashes and no en dashes anywhere. Note that brand.ts ruleCheckCopy only tests for the em dash, so the en dash is a human-enforced rule for now.
conventions.ask: Which CTA verb a caption uses. `answer` pairs with the cliffhanger ending (the current default, so most of the bank), `score` pairs with full-reveal, `either` works under both. Mirrors defaults.ts captionAsk.
conventions.requires: Render props a line depends on to stay true. null means unconditional. A selector MUST honour this: picking a `{ending: cliffhanger}` line for a full-reveal arm turns a self-verifiable line into a false one.

stated-difficulty-stat.priority: FIRST. This is the named pattern and the highest-value untested idea available to us.
stated-difficulty-stat.source_claim: Authority via statistics plus exclusivity of success. The pack's own labels: 'Authority via statistics', 'Exclusivity effect: being in the minority feels powerful', 'Social contrast: makes action feel like elite behavior'.
stated-difficulty-stat.what_we_test: Leading with a specific failure rate about the question itself, spoken and on the plate, before the question is asked.
stated-difficulty-stat.hypothesis: A number does two jobs a soft framing cannot. It sets a concrete bar the viewer can measure themselves against in under a second, and it converts watching into a status test. The pack's strongest single device is the SPLIT construction ('90% will scroll, will you be the 10%?'), which fuses the stat with an identity dare, and it maps onto a quiz better than onto anything the pack was actually written for.

sub_shapes.split-the-audience: Only 8% get this. Are you one? (the pack's best transferable device)
sub_shapes.ratio: Nine in ten get this one wrong.
sub_shapes.option-decoy: Nine in ten pick {WRONG}. (requires a `fill`, see conventions)

stated-difficulty-stat.note_on_supply: The pack named this pattern; it did not supply a bank of it. Only 69 of 3750 entries carry any number, 26 of those are creator-result brags, and most of the rest are world-fact trivia. The difficulty-framing subset is roughly six distinct constructions. Every line below is authored by us against those shapes.

declared-difficulty.source_claim: Attention bias / curiosity through contradiction. The source pack's framing is that flagging an item as hard makes the viewer commit before they know why.
declared-difficulty.what_we_test: The SAME job as stated-difficulty-stat with the number removed: our opinion that the puzzle is hard, stated as an opinion.
declared-difficulty.hypothesis: This is the designated control for the numeric arm and the most informative pairing in the bank. Same slot, same intent, same brand register, one variable. If the number is doing the work, this loses; if 'sneaky' does it just as well, the number is decoration and we learn that cheaply. It is also verbatim host vocabulary, so it cannot lose for sounding foreign.

challenge-dare.source_claim: Challenge format sparks engagement; social identity bias (being in the minority who can do it feels good).
challenge-dare.what_we_test: A direct second-person dare instead of a neutral invitation.
challenge-dare.hypothesis: A dare recruits ego. It is also the closest mechanism to the brand's existing binary, so it should be the cheapest to make sound native.

expectation-violation.source_claim: Expectation violation / belief disruption. The source's highest-frequency curiosity device.
expectation-violation.what_we_test: Telling the viewer the question is not what it looks like, without telling them anything about the specific item.
expectation-violation.hypothesis: A warning that the surface reading is wrong buys a second look, and a second look is a solve attempt.

pattern-interrupt.source_claim: Pattern interrupt plus commitment cue. The source's single largest family of scroll-stoppers.
pattern-interrupt.what_we_test: An explicit imperative to stop scrolling, versus starting on content.
pattern-interrupt.hypothesis: Weakest prior of the six. It is the most burned-out device on the platform and the least game-show. Worth testing precisely because it is the default advice and we should know whether it is dead.

time-pressure.source_claim: Time pressure effect; time constraint plus curiosity.
time-pressure.what_we_test: Front-loading the format's own constraint (five seconds a question) as the hook.
time-pressure.hypothesis: Our countdown is already the most game-show thing about us and it is currently a surprise. Announcing it sets a contract the viewer can accept in under a second.

open-loop.source_claim: Zeigarnik effect. Open a loop, withhold closure.
open-loop.what_we_test: Announcing the cliffhanger at the top rather than discovering it at the bottom.
open-loop.hypothesis: Genuinely uncertain and worth knowing: telling people the payoff is withheld could buy the watch, or could remove the reason to stay. The cliffhanger ending is already the default, so this tests the ANNOUNCEMENT, not the ending.

identity-ingroup.source_claim: Affinity targeting / identity affirmation. Speaks to a valued self-image.
identity-ingroup.what_we_test: Addressing a self-selecting group rather than everyone.
identity-ingroup.hypothesis: Caption-only. Twelve source hooks of this shape, all needing a second clause to land, which is too slow for a three-second window but fine in text.

settle-it.source_claim: Tribal validation / polarizing engagement. The source's comment-farming family.
settle-it.what_we_test: Inviting disagreement in the comments rather than asking for a score.
settle-it.hypothesis: Caption-only, and the one mechanism aimed at comments rather than retention. Comments are our thinnest signal (10 across the whole database) and they feed the auto-replier, so cheap volume here is worth something even if reach does not move.

openings.source: adapted from '99% will wait, 1% will act, who are you?' (FOMO & Urgency), psychology 'Social contrast'. Attaches the scarcity to a clean score of three, which is the one number in the format everybody understands.

openings.vo: Nine in ten get this one wrong.
openings.source: ratio form of the same claim. Included because a ratio reads faster on a plate than a percentage and lands harder spoken, which is worth a separate read.

openings.vo: Seventy percent get this one wrong.
openings.source: the deliberate MODERATE-magnitude entry. Same construction as open-stat-02 with a believable number instead of a dramatic one, so the arm can eventually tell us whether extremity helps or costs credibility.

openings.vo: Nine out of ten people pick {WRONG}.

fill.{WRONG}: any option letter that is NOT the answer. The selector knows the answer, so this is a lookup, not a judgement. Never leave the placeholder unresolved and never let it resolve to the correct letter, or the hook contradicts its own reveal.

openings.source: the option-decoy shape, requested by name. No direct source line; built from the pack's ratio construction plus the specificity principle it labels 'Data + shock'.

openings.vo: Heads up. This one is sneaky.
openings.source: adapted from 'Watch closely, most people miss this' (Curiosity & Open-Loop); the population half was cut, the attention half kept. 'sneaky' is verbatim host vocabulary.

openings.vo: Fair warning. The last one is mean.
openings.source: adapted from 'Most people never master this' (Authority & Expertise); reframed from a claim about people into an apology about our own puzzle.

openings.vo: Okay, this one is tricky. Good luck.
openings.source: the host's own verbatim line 'and this one is tricky!' from brand-voice-examples vo-question, promoted to the opener slot.

openings.vo: Warning. Question three bites.
openings.source: adapted from 'This blind spot ruins most people' (Problem-Solution); the ruin is transferred from the viewer to the question.

openings.vo: Bet you can't get all three.
openings.source: 'I bet you can't do this' (Relatable Hooks), psychology 'Challenge format = sparks engagement'. Kept almost intact because it was already assertion-free.

openings.vo: Think you're a smart fella? Prove it.
openings.source: 'If you're a [target audience], you're not going to like this' (Educational); the identity call was kept, the threat dropped, and the brand binary substituted.

openings.vo: Three questions. Beat all three.
openings.source: 'Your move. Clock's ticking' (FOMO & Urgency) stripped to the dare. The count is read off the render props.

openings.vo: Get all three and you're certified.
openings.source: 'Only a few people will act, be one of them' (FOMO & Urgency); the scarcity claim was replaced with our own scoring rule, which is a rule we define rather than a fact we assert.

openings.vo: This one looks easy. Does it though?
openings.source: 'This looks simple, but it's not' (Curiosity & Open-Loop). The flat contradiction was turned into a question so it asserts nothing about the item.

openings.vo: Read it twice. We'll wait.
openings.source: 'Don't judge this too early' (Curiosity & Open-Loop), rewritten as an instruction, which is the assertion-free form of the same nudge.

openings.vo: Don't answer too fast.

plate.title: DON'T RUSH IT
plate.subtitle: rushing is a fart smella move

openings.source: 'At first glance, this looks normal, but it's not' (Curiosity & Intrigue). Kept the instruction, dropped the assertion, landed it on the brand binary.

openings.vo: Feels too easy, right?
openings.source: 'This is not what you think' (Curiosity & Open-Loop) as a question. The shortest opener in the bank, which is the point of having it.

openings.vo: Stop scrolling. Three questions.
openings.source: 'Stop scrolling if you're ready to level up' (Motivational), psychology 'Pattern interrupt + commitment cue'. The self-improvement half was cut.

openings.vo: Don't scroll past this one.
openings.source: 'Don't scroll, this is urgent' (Fear & Urgency) with the manufactured urgency removed.

openings.vo: Thumb down. Brain on.
openings.source: 'Want it? Then stop scrolling' (Motivational) compressed to four words. Playful and a bit dumb on purpose, which is the brand.

openings.vo: Freeze. Question one.
openings.source: 'While you scroll, your chance is slipping' (FOMO & Urgency) reduced to the interrupt, because the loss framing is neither kid-safe in tone nor true.

openings.vo: Five seconds a question. Go.
openings.source: 'The clock is ticking' (FOMO & Urgency) made concrete with our actual countdown value.

openings.vo: Clock's already running.
openings.source: 'Your move. Clock's ticking' (FOMO & Urgency). The only unconditional line in this mechanism, so it survives any tempo arm.

openings.vo: Three questions. Fifteen seconds total.
openings.source: 'This took me 10 years, you get it in 60 seconds' (Authority & Expertise) with the authority brag removed. The number is arithmetic on our own render props, which is what an honest number looks like here.

openings.vo: No pausing. No googling. Go.
openings.source: 'If you can't explain it in 30 seconds, you can't sell it' (Sales & Persuasion) reduced to its constraint-setting move, which is the transferable part.

openings.vo: Stay to the end. There's a catch.
openings.source: 'Wait until you see the ending' (Curiosity & Open-Loop), psychology 'Zeigarnik effect'. The catch is real: the cliffhanger default withholds the last answer.

openings.vo: We're not telling you the last answer.
openings.source: 'I shouldn't be saying this, but' (Curiosity & Open-Loop) inverted: instead of teasing hidden knowledge, we admit up front that we are withholding it.

openings.vo: Two answers. One secret.
openings.source: 'Here's the part nobody talks about' (Curiosity & Open-Loop) made literal and countable.

openings.vo: Question three doesn't get an answer.
openings.source: 'What happens next will surprise you' (Curiosity & Open-Loop) replaced with the specific, true version, because specificity is the half of that hook that is not a lie.

provenance.external_source: '5,000 Viral Hooks with Psychology' (paid pack, ~3,750 entries, ~3,508 unique after removing an ~800-line block duplicated between the Educational and Relatable sections). Structure is per-hook: a templated hook line, a worked example, and a one-line psychology label. The labels are ad hoc rather than a taxonomy (roughly 2,000 distinct label strings), so the mechanisms above are our consolidation of them, not the pack's.
provenance.why_nothing_is_pasted: The pack is written for talking-head personal-brand creators. Its dominant voice is first-person authority ('I audited 200 accounts', 'my clients') which we structurally cannot use. Every line here was rewritten against brand/brand-voice.md and the 262-example corpus.

how_thin_the_numeric_family_actually_is.world_fact_trivia: most of the remaining 43 ('78% live paycheck to paycheck', '90% of serotonin is in the gut'). Shocking-stat hooks, not difficulty hooks.
how_thin_the_numeric_family_actually_is.actual_difficulty_framing_constructions: roughly six, and the best of them is the SPLIT form ('90% will scroll, will you be the 10%?').
how_thin_the_numeric_family_actually_is.conclusion: The pack's value on the requested pattern is one idea, not a supply. It named the shape and supplied the split construction; the seven openings and six captions under stated-difficulty-stat are authored by us against those shapes.

what_was_screened_out.product_efficacy_claims: Any number attached to what the product does for the viewer. Where a source hook made an outcome claim worth keeping, the number was moved onto the question's difficulty instead; otherwise it was dropped.
what_was_screened_out.first_person_authority: The whole Authority & Expertise, Case Studies & Proof, and Social Proof sections (roughly 460 entries), including all 26 creator-result numeric brags. No host persona to attach them to.
what_was_screened_out.per_item_contradictions: 'The obvious answer is wrong', 'there is a trap in here'. Dropped for internal consistency: the bank attaches to a randomly selected item, so an uncontrolled pre-judgement of the answer will contradict its own reveal. The one case worth keeping (naming a decoy option) survives as open-stat-07 with a `fill`.
what_was_screened_out.fear_and_loss_framing: The Fear & Urgency and FOMO sections' loss framing ('every second you wait is costing you'). Not kid-safe in tone and reads as smug, which the brand forbids. Note the split-the-audience construction was rescued OUT of this section: the device is good, only its framing was wrong.
what_was_screened_out.off_niche_bulk: Money, fitness, sales, freelancing and business sections. Roughly two thirds of the pack by volume.

known_gaps: NOT WIRED. hermes/src/design.ts sets plan.props.title / plan.props.subtitle from the dimension's `hook`, but hermes/src/render.ts shortProps() does not forward either to the renderer, and remotion/src/full/timeline.ts makes shorts permanently cold-open with no intro segment. The existing `hook-challenge` arm ('ONLY 1% PASS') therefore renders a video identical to control. Wiring the opening surface means (a) forwarding title/subtitle, (b) adding an intro segment to the short timeline, and (c) adding an `intro` beat to narration.ts planBeats. That work is deliberately not in this file.

ONLY 1% PASS is now IN POLICY and is preserved as open-stat-01 rather than retired. It has never actually shipped (it appears only in dimensions.ts and the worktree copies, never in ab-database.json), so wiring the arm will ship it for the first time.

The caption count floor is 30, because publishGate.ts NOVELTY_WINDOW is 30 and caption novelty is exact-match: 30 distinct bodies is the minimum that guarantees no repeat inside the window. There are 36 here. Grow it as posting volume rises.
open-stat-07 is the only entry that is not literally drop-in: its `fill` must be resolved by the selector. Everything else renders as written.

brand.ts ruleCheckCopy does not test for the en dash (U+2013) and has no notion of claim_class. The one rule worth making mechanical is the product-efficacy ban: a regex in gateCopy for a number co-occurring with product or outcome vocabulary (score, smarter, IQ, results, users, players, in a week) would catch the only claim class that actually matters, and would cost about five lines.
